podcast.title: Healthy Lifestyle Choices (1971-2002)
podcast.body: Despite smoking and drinking, Joe Strummer maintained a vegetarian diet since 1971 and regularly ran marathons, practices that made his sudden death from a heart condition particularly unexpected. "Yes, he smoked and drank, but he'd been a vegetarian since 1971. He ran marathons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Meeting Courtney Love (1987)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer befriended Courtney Love in 1987 while filming "Straight to Hell." After production wrapped, Joe purchased a plane ticket for Courtney to return to the States when she couldn't afford to go home. "She enjoyed being friends since 1987 when they made on the set of Straight to Hell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion attempt with Mick Jones (1990)
podcast.body: Around 1990, Mick Jones suggested reforming The Clash, but Joe Strummer's stubbornness prevented it. Joe insisted on the original late 70s/early 80s lineup (Joe, Mick, Paul Simonon, Topper Headon if sober, or Terry Chimes) and the return of former manager Bernie Rhodes, whom the other members refused to work with due to his past lawsuit attempt. "Joe was stubborn. He believed that if the clash were to rise again, it would have to be just as it was back in the late 70s and early 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joining The Pogues (1991)
podcast.body: In 1991, after The Pogues fired their singer Shane McGowan for alcoholism, Joe Strummer was asked to fill in as lead singer, having previously done studio work with the band. "Joe Strummer during his stints as the lead singer with the Pogs in the early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Charitable Requests in Memory (December 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's wife, Lucinda, requested that instead of sending flowers, people donate money in Joe's name to an organization addressing the AIDS crisis in Africa. Fans were also encouraged to plant a tree in his name for the Future Forest's Environmental Charity, a gesture intended to offset pollution from CD manufacturing and disposal. "Instead, she asked that people donate money and Joe's name to an organization dedicated to the AIDS crisis in Africa."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (December 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash died just before Christmas in 2002 from a heart attack. "Joe Strummer of the Clash, heart attack just before Christmas, 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death and Legacy (December 22, 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer died suddenly on December 22, 2002, at the age of 50, from a heart attack, likely due to an unknown hereditary condition, at his home in Somerset, England, shortly after walking his dogs. His death shocked the world and led to reflections on his importance, with some comparing him to Kurt Cobain or Joey Ramone for an entire generation. "Joe was just 50. The world was shocked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Gig with Mick Jones (November 16, 2002)
podcast.body: On November 16, 2002, Joe Strummer and The Mescaleros played a benefit concert for a London fire brigade. Mick Jones, who was in the audience, joined them on stage to perform a couple of songs, marking their first joint performance since 1983. Both agreed the experience "felt very, very, very good," though it was unknowingly Joe's final live performance. "That marked the first time in 1983 that Joe and Mick had performed together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Funeral Procession and Service (December 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's funeral procession traveled through London, intentionally passing by locations where The Clash used to perform. The simple coffin was adorned with stickers saying "vinyl rules" and "question authority asked me anything." A private service was held at the West London Crematorium, attended by the remaining members of The Clash, "the cream of British Rock and Roll," and Courtney Love. Two dozen uniformed firemen, beneficiaries of Joe's last gig, stood at attention, and a fire truck led the procession. "The funeral procession wound its way through London, deliberately passing some of the places where the clash used to play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sudden Death (2002)
podcast.body: On Sunday, December 22, 2002, Joe Strummer died of a heart attack on his kitchen floor in Somerset, England, shortly after returning from a walk with his dog. His death, likely the result of an unknown hereditary condition, occurred when he was just 50 years old, marking the passing of a "founding father of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Sudden Death (December 22, 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer died unexpectedly on Sunday, December 22, 2002, at home after returning from a dog walk. His death was caused by a massive heart attack resulting from his rare, undiagnosed congenital heart condition. "On Sunday, December 22, 2002, Joe took his dog out for a walk, came back, sat down on the couch and died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Aborted Band Projects (Post-Sony Deal)
podcast.body: After his release from Sony, Joe Strummer attempted to form new bands, including an aborted project with a group called Machine and another unsuccessful attempt to collaborate with Bez from Happy Mondays. "There was an aborted attempt with a group called Machine and then Joe tried to get something going with Bez, X of the Happy Mondays, but that didn't work out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Background and Lifestyle Choice
podcast.body: Joe Strummer, despite being the privileged son of a diplomat, intentionally chose to live with his "down-and-up punk friends," embracing a punk lifestyle.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Birth and Early Life
podcast.body: Born John Miller on August 21, 1952, in Ankara, Turkey, Joe Strummer began life as a "well-bred, privately educated member of the British Empire." His father was a foreign service diplomat, leading the family to live in Cyprus, Cairo, and Mexico City by the time John was 10. He and his older brother, David, attended a private boarding school in London before he moved on to art school.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brief Cartooning Ambition
podcast.body: While at art school, Joe Strummer briefly flirted with the idea of becoming a professional cartoonist. However, this ambition was cut short when he was expelled from art school for taking LSD. During this "cartoonist phase," he adopted the name Woody Miller, inspired by the American folk singer Woody Guthrie.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Children with Gay Sultor
podcast.body: Joe Strummer spent many years with Gay Sultor, though they never married. Together, they had two daughters, Jazz Domino Holly and Lola Mabeline. "Joe then spent many years with a woman named Gay Sultor. They never married but they did have two daughters. Jazz Domino Holly and Lola Mabeline."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Comparison to Punk Idols
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's significance to an entire generation of people was directly compared to the impact of figures like Kurt Cobain and Joey Ramone, establishing him as an equally important idol for punk rock fans. "To many Joe Strummer was their equivalent of Kurt Cobain, just as Joey Ramon might have been."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death by Heart Attack
podcast.body: Joe Strummer passed away due to a heart attack. "the heart attack that killed Joe Strummer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Deep-Sea Snail Species
podcast.body: In 2014, Joe Strummer, who died in 2002, had a species of spiky, golf ball-sized sea snails named after him: *Elvini Conca Strummer-I*. These snails inhabit extreme environments near hydrothermal vents in the deep ocean, living at depths of almost 12,000 feet in dark, hot, and acidic conditions. "a new species of Elvini Conca should be named Strummer-I, toughbuggers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diplomat's Son – Real Name John Miller, Born in Ankara, Raised Across Multiple Postings
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's entire punk persona was built on a working-class streetwise identity that contradicted his actual origins. His real name was John Mellor (referred to as John Miller in the podcast). He was born in Ankara, Turkey, while his father, a British diplomat with the Foreign Service, was posted there. His father subsequently received postings to Mexico City, Cairo, and Bonn, West Germany — providing Joe and his brother with security, good schools, and comfortable accommodations. The family eventually settled in Surrey, England, where the boys attended private schools befitting a diplomat's salary. Joe transformed himself into a punk musician via art school and spent the rest of his life distancing Joe Strummer the punk from his privileged origins. "He considered his upbringing to be an embarrassment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Director Alex Cox Collaborations
podcast.body: Joe Strummer formed a strong working relationship with director Alex Cox, leading to several film collaborations. After contributing to the soundtrack of *Sid and Nancy*, Joe was given acting roles in Cox's next two movies, *Walker* (1987) and *Straight to Hell* (1987), for which he also composed the entire score for *Walker*.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Life and Background
podcast.body: Joe Strummer came from a privileged background, as his father was a diplomat. He was born in Turkey and lived in exotic places like Cairo and Mexico City before his family moved to England. He attended private schools and boarding school, and initially wanted to be a cartoonist. "He came from privilege. His dad was a diplomat and little Joe was born in Turkey and lived in exotic places like Cairo and Mexico City before the family moved to England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Ethos and Contradictions
podcast.body: Joe Strummer and The Clash were characterized as idealistic, conflicted, and confused, embodying both reactionary and revolutionary tendencies. They championed the working class and the poor, and "sneered at consumerism and the privileged," yet controversially sold their songs for TV commercials, advertising products like Levi's jeans and Jaguar cars. "They were both a reactionary and revolutionary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Marriage for Citizenship
podcast.body: In 1970, Joe Strummer married Pamela Muleman from South Africa for 400 pounds, a sum she paid him so she could obtain British citizenship. He used the money to purchase the first real guitar he ever owned, and the couple subsequently divorced. "In 1970, Joe married a woman named Pamela Muleman. She was from South Africa and she needed her British citizenship. So Joe married her 400 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Formation of The Mescaleros
podcast.body: Following unsuccessful attempts to form other groups, Joe Strummer successfully assembled a new band he named The Mescaleros, who were noted for being "pretty good," even when performing old Clash songs. "But in the end, he pulled together a band he called the Mescaleros."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Godfather Role
podcast.body: Joe Strummer became the Godfather to British singer Lily Allen. "He had also become Godfather to British singer Lily Allen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Inspirational Figure
podcast.body: For a generation of punk fans, Joe Strummer served as an inspirational figure, holding a similar level of significance as John Lennon did for the preceding generation.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Interviewed by Host
podcast.body: Joe Strummer was among the artists interviewed by the host over the years. "I've had the privilege of talking to a ton of really cool people over the years...Joe Stromer, The Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Later Life and Reunion Prospects
podcast.body: As he grew older, Joe Strummer mellowed somewhat. By late 2002, after many years of rumors and false starts, a reunion of The Clash seemed to be a real possibility.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Learning Guitar and Unique Strumming Style
podcast.body: John Miller didn't seriously pick up a guitar until 1972, at the age of 20. He met busker Timon Dogg at the Green Park Tube Stop in London, who taught him a few elementary chords. Joe later adopted the name Joe Strummer in early 1975 because of his unique guitar strumming method. He was "too lazy" to learn chords "the right way" and found shortcuts, which, while "technically ugly," resulted in a distinctive sound and style.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Loss of Posh Accent
podcast.body: Legend has it that Joe Strummer's ability to enunciate clearly and his "posh boarding school accent" changed forever after he had his teeth kicked in during a pub brawl. This incident is associated with his transition to a more working-class punk image.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mentioned in Rage Against The Machine Liner Notes
podcast.body: Joe Strummer, described as a musician and revolutionary, was acknowledged with "props" in the liner notes of Rage Against The Machine's debut album. "Revolutionaries and musicians like Chuck D and Joe Stromer get props."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Modest Lifestyle
podcast.body: Even at the time of his death, Joe Strummer lived a low-key and modest life with his second wife, Lucinda. "Even at the time of his death, Joe was low-key and living very modestly with his second wife, Lucinda."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Musical Influences
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's early musical heroes included The Beatles and The Beach Boys. He also developed a strong interest in American folk singer Woody Guthrie, to the extent that he adopted the name Woody Miller during his cartoonist phase. His later, more significant influences, which he described as "Black men," encompassed Canadian Ronnie Hawkins, blues, R&B, Bo Diddley, Chuck Berry, and various reggae artists like Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, Toots and the Maytals, Desmond Dekker, and Burning Spear.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Path to Punk Rock
podcast.body: Two significant factors led Joe Strummer to become a punk rocker: his discovery of rock music around age 10, and the suicide of his brother, David. Following these events, Joe actively turned his back on his upper-middle-class upbringing and immersed himself in the punk rock lifestyle. "The things that put Joe in the road to being a punk were A, his discovery of rock music at about age 10, and B, his brother David's suicide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Political Activism
podcast.body: Beyond his musical contributions, Joe Strummer was highly political, actively campaigning against issues such as poverty and racism, and consistently supporting labor groups.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Record Label Dispute with Sony (1990s)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer was in a nearly decade-long dispute with his record label (later identified as Sony). The label was reluctant to fund another album, fearing the returns wouldn't cover expenses or Joe's advance, and viewing him as "over." This "Mexican standoff" lasted eight years, ending with a compromise where Sony released him from his contract on the condition that if The Clash ever reunited, they would record for Sony. "This explains why there were no Strummer solo records for nearly a decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Redefining Punk Rock
podcast.body: As a member of The Clash, Joe Strummer was pivotal in expanding the definition of punk rock, moving it beyond its basic "three chords and an attitude roots" to incorporate more complex themes and sounds.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Singing for The Pogues
podcast.body: Joe Strummer sang for The Pogues at one point after the breakup of The Clash. This engagement highlights his continued involvement in the music scene and his collaborations with other influential bands.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Starbucks Street Performance (Toronto)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer once arrived late, hung over, and grumpy to a live radio broadcast in Toronto. Frustrated by the noise preventing him from tuning his battered guitar, he abruptly left the studio and performed solo for passersby outside a crowded Starbucks store on Yonge Street. "Up there on Young Street, Interrano was one of the greatest living punks playing solo for people as they walked by."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Undiagnosed Congenital Heart Condition (Intramural Coronary Artery)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer had an extremely rare, undiagnosed congenital heart condition called an intramural coronary artery, where an errant artery grew through his heart muscle. This condition quietly worsened, eventually constricting the artery and triggering a massive heart attack; only about 100 similar cases have ever been recorded. "He had something called an intramural coronary artery, a congenital condition that quietly got worse. This errant artery grew through the heart muscle. It got bigger and bigger until the artery squeezed shut, triggering a massive heart attack."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

xref.title: Backstage Window Encounter (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash recounted how he, Johnny Rotten, and members of the Sex Pistols met The Ramones backstage at the Roundhouse by throwing a rock at a window. Johnny Ramone stuck his head out, and the British punks introduced themselves, being subsequently pulled up through the window in a "human chain" to get in. "And so they kind of formed a sort of human chain and pulled us up through this window. And that was the first time we met him and that was just a really great punk rock moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for British Punk (1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played a pivotal gig at the Roundhouse in London on Sunday, July 4th, 1976, as part of America's Bicentennial. Around 2,000 members of the "infant UK punk community" packed the venue, eager to hear the New York sound. This performance, along with another at Dingwalls, was immensely influential; key figures like Johnny Rotten and Joe Strummer attended soundchecks and shows, stating that the Ramones "turned them on" and "inspired them to form their own bands." The band felt like "royalty" upon arrival, noting the shift from selling out CBGB's to playing for 3,000 kids already "tuned in." "No one could have known it at the time, but this was one of the most influential gigs in the history of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

xref.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Members of the newly formed Clash, including Joe Strummer, were present at The Ramones' July 4, 1976 gig at the Roundhouse in London. Strummer recounted how they got backstage by forming a "human chain" through a window to meet The Ramones, describing it as a "really great punk rock moment." "Members of the newly formed clash, Chrissy Hind of the still unformed pretenders, the damn who would become the first British punk band to release a record, Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Arrested for Stealing a Pillowcase and Towels – Newcastle, June 1977, Fined 100 Pounds
xref.body: On June 11, 1977, Joe Strummer and Topper Headon were in Newcastle. The following night they were arrested on robbery charges for allegedly stealing a pillowcase and several towels from a Holiday Inn. They were supposed to have appeared in court in May 1977 to answer these charges but had simply not turned up. A judge took a dim view of the non-appearance; in the end they were fined 100 pounds each. "I mean, the Clash. They were arrested for stealing a pillowcase."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hepatitis from Gobbing – 1979, Spat in Mouth During Performance
xref.body: In the early British punk scene, audience members competed to spit at bands on stage as a sign of enthusiasm following a newspaper article depicting the practice. During a 1979 Clash performance, Joe Strummer was singing with his mouth open when an audience member's spit landed directly in it. The result was a significant case of hepatitis. The practice of spitting at performers, known as "gobbing," was common enough that performers were routinely covered in phlegm and mucus during shows. "Joe Strummer was singing. His mouth was open and the result was a really nasty case of hepatitis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bernie Rhodes' Re-hiring and Internal Strife (1981)
xref.body: Rhodes was re-hired in 1981 after the band was unsuccessfully managed by Joe Strummer's girlfriend. Upon his return, he actively worked to pit Joe Strummer and Mick Jones against each other, possibly with the goal of becoming the band's musical director. "But then he was re-hired in 1981 after the group was unsuccessfully run by Joe Stromer's girlfriend. And this is where things went wrong again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creative Control Conflict (1981)
xref.body: During the recording of *Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg* in 1981, founding member Mick Jones and Joe Strummer were in conflict over creative control. Jones, along with drummer Topper Heaton, was exploring Dub, Reggae, and world music, leading to longer songs, while Strummer disliked this direction and desired a concise, single album due to the band's debt with CBS. This led to them working in separate studios. "At the time, Mick Jones, the founder of the group, was fighting with Joe Strummer over creative control... it got to the point where Mick was working on material in one studio, and Joe was working on his clash material in another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Debt with Label (1981)
xref.body: The Clash had gone "deep into debt" with their label, CBS, which influenced Joe Strummer's desire for a "nice tight single album" for effective promotion, contrasting with Mick Jones's more sprawling vision for *Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg*. "after going deep into debt with their label, Joe wanted a nice tight single album that CBS could promote effectively."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Claim of "Rock the Casbah" Influence (1982)
xref.body: After a 1982 show in Paris, Rashid Taha, an Algerian singer-songwriter and leader of the French Arab-punk band Residence Permit, gave Joe Strummer a demo cassette. A year later, Taha noted that The Clash's "Rock the Casbah" bore stylistic similarities to his demo, implying a potential influence, though Taha never expressed bitterness and later recorded his own version of the song. "he turned on the radio and heard some song called Rock the Casbah, which stylistically, anyway, sounded an awful lot like some of the stuff on the demo cassette that he gave Joe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (1982)
xref.body: Joe Strummer, a key voice of the British punk explosion, inexplicably vanished on April 26, 1982, the night before The Clash was due to leave on a major tour, forcing the tour to be scrapped. He was gone for eight full weeks, showing up suddenly in mid-May 1982, offering various unconfirmed explanations like running the Paris marathon or helping a girlfriend's mother out of jail, leading to speculation about a publicity stunt or burnout; this vanishing act retrospectively marked the beginning of the end for the band. "Joe Strummer, one of the voices of the whole British punk explosion had inexplicably disappeared, vanished."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Possible Influence from Rashid Taha (1982)
xref.body: After a 1982 show in Paris, Algerian singer-songwriter Rashid Taha, leader of the French Arab-punk band Residence Permit, gave Joe Strummer a demo cassette. A year later, Taha noted stylistic similarities between his demo and "Rock the Casbah," leading to speculation about whether The Clash drew inspiration from his material, though Taha never expressed bitterness and even covered the song himself. "Was Rock the Casbah inspired by what was handed to Joe on that sidewalk that night? Maybe."

xref.title: Firing of Mick Jones (September 1, 1983) – Manager-Engineered Split That Destroyed the Band
xref.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes had spent years pitting Joe Strummer against Mick Jones, encouraging Joe to fire him. On September 1, 1983, Mick Jones's departure was announced in a formal "Clash Communiqué" stating he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the Clash." The resulting lineup recorded the critically panned *Cut the Crap* (1985), featuring two new members, after which the Clash simply dissolved with no official announcement. Mick Jones went on to major success with Big Audio Dynamite, while Strummer spent over a decade in record-company limbo and never again achieved the stature he had with the Clash. "Firing Mick Jones? Terrible. Joe Strummer thought he knew better than Mick, and he ended up paying for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mick Jones' Dismissal (September 1, 1983)
xref.body: Guitarist Mick Jones was fired on September 1, 1983, a decision announced via a "clash communique" that stated he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the clash." This followed increasing difficulties, including being late for rehearsals and recording, refusing tours, and his relationship with Joe Strummer deteriorating due to Bernie Rhodes's machinations. Joe Strummer expressed frustration about having to "beg him to play the guitar," comparing the situation to "dragging a dead dog around." "It was September 1st, 1983, and his firing was announced in what was called a clash communique."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Death (December 2002)
xref.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash died just before Christmas in 2002 from a heart attack. "Joe Strummer of the Clash, heart attack just before Christmas, 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Rock the Casbah" Lyric Reference
xref.body: The Clash's song "Rock the Casbah" contains a line that references Bernie Rhodes, specifically Joe Strummer singing: "now the king told his boogeyman, you have to let that ragged drop." This lyric is interpreted as Strummer referring to a situation where the record company insisted on dropping the eight-minute song "Sean Flynn" from the *Combat Rock* album, and Bernie Rhodes was the one who agreed to its removal.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Awareness of Impending Death
xref.body: Unlike Joe Strummer, Lou Reed was aware that he was going to die, facing a prolonged period of declining health. "Unlike Joe Strummer, Lou Reed knew he was going to die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Backstage Anecdote at The Roundhouse
xref.body: Joe Strummer recounted an incident at The Roundhouse where he, John Z, and some of the Sex Pistols threw a rock at Johnny Ramone's backstage window to get in. Johnny Ramone eventually stuck his head out, and the future punk icons were pulled up through the window in a "human chain," a memorable "punk rock moment." "I think Johnny Ramones stuck his head out and went, and we met, hey, this is the clash and this is the business and we needed to get in and so they kind of formed a sort of human chain and pulled us up through this window and that was the first time we met him and it was just a really great punk rock moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band's Demise from Internal Politics
xref.body: The Clash ultimately imploded due to internal politics, with their true demise occurring after Joe Strummer fired Mick Jones, a co-founder of the band. "The clash, a band that was eventually torn apart by internal politics, but their real demise came after Joe Strummer fired Mick Jones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Catalyst for British Punk Explosion
xref.body: The Ramones' two London gigs in July 1976 are considered foundational for the British punk rock explosion. Major figures like Johnny Rotten, Sid Vicious, Joe Strummer, Chrissy Hynde, The Damned, and Billy Idol were in attendance and were profoundly "transformed by what they saw and heard," inspiring them to form their own bands. "Over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cultural Icon of Political Punk
xref.body: The Clash, particularly through Joe Strummer, were regarded as the quintessential political and activist punk band, embodying a defiant spirit that resonated with millions worldwide and refused to compromise. "He was the political punk, the activist punk, the punk that refused to bend. For millions around the world, he was the guy who embodied the best of the punk spirit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Daughter's Crafting and Gardening Skills
xref.body: Joe Strummer's daughter, Jazz Domino Holly, is noted for her craftiness. She is a knitter, makes duvets, cooks, and is an avid gardener. She even authored a handbook covering these subjects. "she makes duvetes, cooks, and is an avid gardener."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Diverse Musical Inspirations
xref.body: His inspirations include Jimi Hendrix, Joe Strummer, Captain Beefheart, Frank Zappa, Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order, and significantly, John McGeoch of Siouxsie and the Banshees, admired for his varied soundscapes. "And who does he look for for inspiration? Well, we talked about Hendrix, but also Joe Strummer, Captain B. Fart, Frank Zappa, loose legend Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Family Background and Influences
xref.body: Florence's father, Nick, was an "old punk" who had associations with Joe Strummer before The Clash formed, and later became an ad executive for Aero Chocolate Bars, resembling Andy Warhol. Her paternal grandfather hung out with the Warhol crowd at Studio 54, and another grandfather, a deputy editor of the Daily Telegraph, gave her the soundtrack to *The Rocky Horror Picture Show*, which became her first favorite record and sparked a crush on its creator, Richard O'Brien, at age 10. "And then there's her father, Nick. He was an old punk who once hung out with Joe Strummer in the days before he joined the clash."

The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer Adopts Mohawk After Taxi Driver
xref.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash was inspired by Robert De Niro's Mohawk in the 1976 movie "Taxi Driver" and subsequently shaved his own head into the style, initiating a trend for punks and their admirers to emulate and develop. "So Joe shaved his head in a Mohawk, thereby sitting up a trend for all punks and punk admirers to copy and evolve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Background
xref.body: The last member to join the group was Joe Strummer, whose real name was John Millers. He was a "refugee" from a pub rock band called The 101ers and insisted on being addressed by his new moniker. Millers, the son of an international diplomat, had a somewhat "posh" upbringing but intentionally abandoned it to become a busker. He earned the name "Strummer" due to the intense ferocity with which he played his guitar. "The last member of the group to join was a refugee from a pub rock band called the 101ers, and he insisted on being addressed as Joe Strummer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Background and Joining
xref.body: The singer, Joe Strummer, was a busker with a "secretly posh background" as the son of a diplomat. He was the last member to join, convinced to defect from a pub rock band called The 101ers. "He called himself Joe Strummer, and he was the last to join when he was convinced to defect from a pub rock band called the 101ers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Cause of Death
xref.body: Joe Strummer died on December 22nd, 2002, from an intra-mural coronary artery, a rare genetic condition where a main blood vessel of the heart grows within the muscle wall, eventually squeezing shut and causing a fatal heart attack. "The cause of death was an intra-mural coronary artery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Last Performance
xref.body: Joe Strummer's final performance occurred on November 24th, 2002, with his band The Mescaleros at Liverpool University, just one month before his sudden passing. "On November 24th, 2002, John is banned the Mescalero's play to show at Liverpool University."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's London Marathon
xref.body: While the myth of Joe Strummer running a Paris marathon in a chicken suit is false, he did genuinely run the London marathon. His official time was four hours and forty-three minutes, and he accomplished this impressive feat without any proper training. "Joe most certainly ran the London marathon and his official time was four hours and forty three minutes and that he did it without any proper training."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Marathon Myth
xref.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes created a false story in 1982 that Joe Strummer had disappeared and his safety was feared, ahead of the "Combat Rock" album release. Joe genuinely took a vacation to Paris, where he reportedly ran a local marathon, with varying times of "four hours and thirty minutes" or "three hours and twenty minutes" reported, and claims of drinking ten pints of beer the night before. This story mutated into the myth that he ran a marathon in Paris dressed in a chicken suit, which is untrue, though he did run the London marathon in four hours and forty-three minutes without proper training. "Somehow this mutated into the story of Joe running the marathon in disguise and eventually that disguise became a chicken suit. Sorry to say, but it's not true."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Rap Influence
xref.body: During the period between studio sessions, Joe Strummer spent time exploring New York City, where he became acquainted with and influenced by early rap sounds, particularly Grandmaster Flash, which then permeated into their song "The Magnificent Seven." "Joe Strummer had plenty of time to wander New York where he started to pick up on the sound to rap. Grandmaster Flash became a favorite. And this song definitely features those early rap influences."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Sudden Passing
xref.body: Joe Strummer died quickly and without drama; he went for a dog walk, returned home, passed through the kitchen, and then sat on the sofa where he passed away. "Joe's death was quick and without any drama. He went out to walk the dog, came home, went through the kitchen, sat on the sofa, and that was it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Unexpected Death
xref.body: Joe Strummer's death came as a complete surprise, given his lifestyle that included running marathons and being a vegetarian since 1971, despite being a smoker and enjoying a drink. "No one saw this coming. Yes, he was a smoker. Yes, he enjoyed a drink. But he also ran marathons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Last Performance with Joe Strummer
xref.body: The Mescaleros played their final show with Joe Strummer at Liverpool University on November 24th, 2002, just a month before his death. "On November 24th, 2002, John is banned the Mescalero's play to show at Liverpool University."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lifelong "Ticking Time Bomb"
xref.body: Joe Strummer lived his entire life with this undetected genetic condition, which acted as a "ticking time bomb" in his chest, capable of causing sudden death at any moment. "For his entire life, Joe had this ticking time bomb in his chest that could have gone off at any moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Liner Notes Thank Yous
xref.body: The debut album's liner notes feature an extensive list of acknowledgments, including Beto (Zach Dela Roka's father, an artist who destroyed his paintings during a nervous breakdown) and revolutionary musicians such as Chuck D and Joe Strummer. "Beto is Zack's dad, the artist who went crazy in Burdala's paintings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mohawk Popularized in Music by Joe Strummer
xref.body: While the Mohawk's origins are linked to a Robert De Niro film, Joe Strummer of The Clash is widely recognized as the individual who popularized the haircut within the music industry. "The clash featuring Joe Strummer, the popularizer of the Mohawk haircut in music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rarity of Joe Strummer's Condition
xref.body: At the time of Joe Strummer's death, his condition, intra-mural coronary artery disease, was extremely rare, with only 100 reported cases in the entire history of medicine. "At the time of Joe's death on December 22nd, 2002, only 100 cases of intra-mural coronary artery disease had been reported in the entire history of medicine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relationship with Joe Strummer
xref.body: Paloma Romero was romantically involved with John Miller, who later became known as Joe Strummer. This connection highlights her presence within the tight-knit early punk community in the UK. "She had a boyfriend named John Miller, who later changed his name to Joe Strummer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

xref.title: Shane MacGowan's Early Punk Anecdote
xref.body: Co-founder Shane MacGowan, a devoted hardcore punk fan, famously had part of his ear bitten off during a Clash show in 1976. A newspaper photo the following day captured Shane holding his ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, accompanied by the headline "Cannibalism at Clash Gig." "They were founded by Shane McGowan, a hard-drinking hardcore punk fan, who once had part of his ear bitten off during a clash show in 1976. The newspaper, the next day carried a photo of Shane holding his right ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, and the headline read Cannibalism at Clash Gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Strumberville Trustee
xref.body: Jazz Domino Holly is one of the trustees of Strumberville, a charitable foundation established in Joe Strummer's name. The foundation aims to encourage the creation of new music and helps kids channel their energies into music and being in bands. "Jazz is a trustee too."

xref.title: Tumultuous Career and Split
xref.body: The Pogues had a critically acclaimed but highly tumultuous career. Shane MacGowan was at one point kicked out of the band and temporarily replaced by Joe Strummer, only to be welcomed back later. The band experienced breakups and long hiatuses, ultimately splitting permanently in 2014 when Shane MacGowan's struggles with drinking and drug problems became unmanageable. "The pokes would go on to have a critically acclaimed but tumultuous career, which would see Shane kicked out replaced by Joe Strummer of all people. And then welcome back in. They were breakups, long hiatus and finally a permanent split in 2014 when Shane could no longer outrun his drinking and drug problems."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Undetectable Condition
xref.body: Joe Strummer's fatal heart condition would not typically be detected through standard medical tests and would only show up during a very proper and in-depth cardiac examination. "This is something that you would never specifically test for."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
